lessons.lessonTitle: Lesson 1: Web Architecture & Client-Server Communication Model

questions.question: What is the primary role of a DNS (Domain Name System) server in web architecture?
options: Rendering DOM trees and executing JavaScript code on client machines
Storing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript source files directly on edge web servers
Translating human-readable domain names (e.g., example.com) into numerical IP addresses
Encrypting HTTP request payloads before transmission over the public Internet
questions.explanation: DNS acts as the Internet's address book, translating domain names like 'google.com' into machine-routable IP addresses like '142.250.190.46'.

questions.question: Which default TCP port numbers are standard for unencrypted HTTP and encrypted HTTPS traffic, respectively?
options: Port 22 for HTTP and Port 80 for HTTPS
Port 80 for HTTP and Port 443 for HTTPS
Port 21 for HTTP and Port 443 for HTTPS
Port 8080 for HTTP and Port 8443 for HTTPS
questions.explanation: Standard web protocols use TCP port 80 for standard HTTP traffic and port 443 for SSL/TLS encrypted HTTPS traffic.

questions.question: In the TCP 3-way handshake used to establish a reliable connection between client and server, what is the exact order of packet flags sent?
options: SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK
PING -> PONG -> ACK
ACK -> SYN -> SYN-ACK
SYN -> ACK -> FIN
questions.explanation: The TCP handshake begins with the client sending a SYN packet, the server replying with SYN-ACK, and the client confirming with an ACK packet before data transmission begins.

questions.question: Which HTTP method is considered both safe (does not alter server state) and idempotent (multiple identical requests yield the same outcome)?
options: GET
POST
CONNECT
PATCH
questions.explanation: GET and HEAD are both safe and idempotent because retrieving a resource does not modify server state and calling it repeatedly produces identical results without side effects.

questions.question: What does the HTTP status code 304 'Not Modified' indicate to the client?
options: The server encountered a temporary internal error and cannot process the request
The client is unauthorized and must provide valid authentication credentials
The requested resource has not changed since the version specified in the client's cache headers (e.g., If-None-Match / ETag), so the browser should use its cached copy
The requested URL has permanently moved to a new destination URI
questions.explanation: Status code 304 informs the browser that its cached copy of the resource is still fresh based on validation headers (like ETag or If-Modified-Since), saving bandwidth by not resending the response body.

questions.question: Why is HTTP described as a 'stateless' protocol?
options: The protocol cannot send binary data such as images or video streams
Servers are legally prohibited from caching user data across sessions
Each request from a client is treated as completely independent, with the server retaining no memory of past requests by default
Clients must re-establish a brand new TCP connection for every single asset requested
questions.explanation: Statelessness means the server does not retain session context between transactions; state must be maintained explicitly using cookies, tokens, or sessions.

questions.question: Which sequence accurately depicts the Critical Rendering Path executed by a web browser?
options: DOM Construction -> Paint -> Layout -> CSSOM Construction -> Compositing
CSSOM Construction -> Paint -> Render Tree -> Layout -> DOM Construction
HTML parsing -> DOM Construction + CSSOM Construction -> Render Tree -> Layout (Reflow) -> Paint -> Compositing
JavaScript Execution -> Layout -> DOM Construction -> Paint -> CSSOM Construction
questions.explanation: The browser parses HTML to build the DOM and CSS to build the CSSOM, combines them into a Render Tree, computes exact positions in Layout, paints pixels, and composites layers onto screen.

questions.question: What is the key difference between loading an external script with 'async' versus 'defer' in HTML5?
options: 'async' scripts execute as soon as they finish downloading (interrupting HTML parsing), while 'defer' scripts execute only after the entire HTML document is parsed, in order
'defer' executes immediately when encountered, whereas 'async' waits for user interaction
'async' scripts only work for inline scripts, whereas 'defer' is required for external URLs
'defer' scripts block HTML parsing during download, whereas 'async' scripts never download in parallel
questions.explanation: Both attributes download scripts asynchronously in the background, but 'async' runs immediately upon download (potentially blocking parsing), while 'defer' guarantees execution in source order after DOM parsing finishes.

questions.question: What is the primary function of a Reverse Proxy (e.g., Nginx, HAProxy) in web architecture?
options: To inspect and filter outgoing traffic initiated by internal employees within a corporate intranet
To sit in front of web/application servers to handle load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and routing client requests
To compile JavaScript code into native machine code directly on client devices
To replace relational database storage engines with file system caches
questions.explanation: A reverse proxy sits in front of backend servers to intercept incoming client requests, performing load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and security filtering.

questions.question: When a browser makes a cross-origin HTTP request with custom headers or methods other than GET/POST/HEAD, what does it send first?
options: A TCP RESET packet to test if the remote firewall is open
A WebSocket upgrade handshake request to verify network latency
A preliminary GET request containing the user's plain-text session cookie
A Preflight request using the HTTP 'OPTIONS' method to check server CORS permissions
questions.explanation: The browser issues a preflight OPTIONS request containing Origin and Access-Control headers to verify if the server permits the cross-origin operation before sending the actual request.

questions.question: Which HTTP status code series represents Client Errors, such as malformed requests, unauthorized access, or non-existent routes?
questions.explanation: 4xx status codes indicate client-side errors (e.g., 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found).

questions.question: What is the key advantage of WebSockets over traditional HTTP polling for real-time bidirectional applications?
options: WebSockets maintain a persistent, full-duplex TCP connection with minimal frame overhead after an initial HTTP handshake
WebSockets do not require any network ports or TCP connections
WebSockets automatically encrypt all data without needing TLS certificates
WebSockets guarantee zero packet loss over unreliable cellular networks
questions.explanation: WebSockets upgrade an HTTP connection to a persistent, bi-directional, full-duplex TCP channel, eliminating the latency and overhead of continuous HTTP request/response cycles.

questions.question: What HTTP header does a server send to tell the browser not to cache a response under any circumstances?
options: Cache-Control: no-store
Cache-Control: max-age=0
Pragma: public
Cache-Control: no-cache
questions.explanation: 'no-store' directs the browser and intermediate proxies never to store any version of the response in cache. 'no-cache' allows caching but forces revalidation before reuse.

questions.question: In the URL 'https://api.example.com:8080/v1/users?role=admin#section2', which component represents the query parameters?
options: api.example.com
role=admin
#section2
questions.explanation: In a URL, the query string follows the '?' symbol (here 'role=admin'), while '#section2' is the fragment/hash identifier.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 regarding request handling?
options: HTTP/2 only supports plain text payloads and disallows binary file transfers
HTTP/2 introduces binary framing and multiplexing, allowing multiple bidirectional streams over a single TCP connection without Head-of-Line blocking at the application layer
HTTP/2 abandons TCP completely and runs exclusively over UDP
HTTP/2 eliminates all request headers to reduce bandwidth consumption
questions.explanation: HTTP/2 multiplexes multiple requests and responses over a single TCP connection using binary frames, solving HTTP/1.1's application-layer Head-of-Line blocking.

questions.question: What is the role of a Content Delivery Network (CDN) in modern web architecture?
options: Compiling Python or Java backend code into executable binaries on the fly
Preventing all client-side JavaScript execution to enhance security
Managing database transactions and enforcing ACID compliance
Distributing cached static assets across geographically dispersed edge servers to reduce latency and origin server load
questions.explanation: CDNs store static assets (images, stylesheets, scripts) on edge servers located geographically close to users, drastically cutting latency and reducing origin server load.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the difference between an Application Server (e.g., Gunicorn, Uvicorn, Node.js) and a Web Server (e.g., Nginx, Apache)?
options: There is no difference; both terms refer to the exact same software component
Web servers parse SQL queries directly, while application servers handle DNS routing
Application servers only run on mobile phones, whereas web servers only run in physical cloud datacenters
Web servers specialize in serving static files and routing traffic, whereas application servers execute dynamic server-side application logic and database interactions
questions.explanation: Web servers (Nginx/Apache) handle static files, SSL termination, and reverse proxy routing, while application servers execute dynamic programming logic (Python/Django/Node.js).

questions.question: Which HTTP status code is returned when a server acting as a gateway or proxy receives an invalid or no response from an upstream server?
options: 504 Gateway Timeout
502 Bad Gateway
500 Internal Server Error
404 Not Found
questions.explanation: 502 Bad Gateway occurs when an intermediary proxy (like Nginx) receives an invalid or dropped response from the upstream application server (like Gunicorn/Node).

questions.question: What is the Same-Origin Policy (SOP) enforced by modern web browsers?
options: A rule that forces every web server to share its database credentials with clients
A network restriction preventing a computer from opening multiple browser tabs simultaneously
A core security mechanism that restricts scripts on one origin from accessing or reading sensitive DOM/data on a different origin (protocol, domain, or port mismatch)
A policy requiring all web pages to use the same CSS styling framework
questions.explanation: Same-Origin Policy isolates potentially malicious documents, preventing scripts on `site-a.com` from reading cookies or DOM data belonging to `site-b.com`.

questions.question: How does Server-Side Rendering (SSR) differ from a Client-Side Rendered Single Page Application (SPA)?
options: SSR does not allow the use of any CSS or styling on web pages
SSR runs exclusively on client web browsers without needing any server hardware
SPAs cannot communicate with backend APIs or databases
SSR generates the complete HTML page on the server for each request, whereas SPAs deliver a minimal HTML shell and render UI components dynamically in the browser via JavaScript
questions.explanation: SSR builds full HTML markup on the server before sending it to the client (improving initial page load and SEO), while SPAs download a bundle and build the DOM in the browser via JS.

lessons.lessonTitle: Lesson 2: HTML5 Document Structure & Semantic Elements

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the `<!DOCTYPE html>` declaration at the beginning of an HTML file?
options: To allocate memory in the browser's JavaScript engine before page load
To specify the server-side database schema for web form submissions
To inform the browser that the document is written in HTML5 and ensure standard rendering mode rather than quirks mode
To link external CSS and JavaScript files to the document automatically
questions.explanation: The `<!DOCTYPE html>` declaration is a document type declaration that tells modern browsers to render the webpage in standards-compliant mode rather than legacy quirks mode.

questions.question: Which `<meta>` tag is essential inside `<head>` to ensure proper scaling and responsive rendering on mobile devices?
options: <meta http-equiv="X-UA-Compatible" content="mobile=1">
<meta name="responsive" content="true">
<meta name="screen-size" content="device-width">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
questions.explanation: The viewport meta tag instructs mobile browsers to set the viewport width to the device screen width and establish an initial 1:1 zoom ratio.

questions.question: Why should web developers use semantic HTML tags (e.g., `<article>`, `<nav>`, `<header>`) instead of generic `<div>` tags everywhere?
options: Semantic tags encrypt all textual content to prevent web scraping
Semantic tags convey structural meaning to search engines, assistive technologies (screen readers), and improve code maintainability
Semantic tags automatically apply modern CSS grid styling without writing any CSS
Browsers execute JavaScript 50% faster when semantic elements are present
questions.explanation: Semantic HTML provides contextual meaning to both search engines (SEO) and accessibility tools (screen readers), making pages accessible and structured.

questions.question: According to HTML5 specifications, how many `<main>` elements should be visible and unique within a single document?
options: As many as desired, with one inside every `<section>` and `<article>`
Exactly one `<main>` element representing the dominant central content of the document
At least two: one for desktop view and one for mobile view
Zero, because `<main>` has been deprecated in HTML5 in favor of `<div id='main'>`
questions.explanation: The `<main>` element represents the dominant content unique to that document and must not be duplicated or nested inside `<article>`, `<aside>`, `<footer>`, `<header>`, or `<nav>`.

questions.question: What is the primary semantic distinction between the `<article>` and `<section>` elements in HTML5?
options: `<article>` is meant for self-contained, independently distributable content (e.g., a blog post or tweet), whereas `<section>` groups thematic content typically with a heading
`<article>` can only contain plain text, whereas `<section>` can only contain images
`<article>` creates a sidebar layout, whereas `<section>` creates full-width containers
`<section>` is used exclusively for page headers, whereas `<article>` is used exclusively for footers
questions.explanation: An `<article>` represents an independent, reusable composition (like a blog post, comment, or product card), whereas a `<section>` represents a standalone generic section of a document grouped by theme.

questions.question: Which HTML5 element is most appropriate for sidebar content, callout boxes, or related links that are tangentially related to the surrounding content?
options: <aside>
<appendix>
<sidebar>
<section type='side'>
questions.explanation: The `<aside>` element represents content tangentially related to the main content around it, such as sidebars, pull quotes, or advertising units.

questions.question: Which element pair is semantically designed to group an illustrative image or code snippet together with its descriptive caption?
options: and
<media> and <caption>
<figure> and <figcaption>
<picture> and <label>
questions.explanation: The `<figure>` element encapsulates self-contained content (like diagrams, photos, or code snippets), and `<figcaption>` provides its associated caption.

questions.question: What is the difference in semantic meaning between `<strong>` vs `<b>`, and `<em>` vs `<i>`?
options: There is no difference in semantics or accessibility between these pairs
`<strong>` and `<em>` convey importance and linguistic emphasis (read with stress by screen readers), while `<b>` and `<i>` represent stylistic bolding/italics without extra semantic importance
`<strong>` and `<em>` are deprecated legacy tags, whereas `<b>` and `<i>` are modern HTML5 elements
`<b>` and `<i>` trigger bold and italic fonts in CSS, while `<strong>` and `<em>` only work in HTML tables
questions.explanation: `<strong>` signifies strong importance/urgency, and `<em>` indicates verbal stress emphasis. `<b>` and `<i>` merely apply typographic style without implying structural weight to assistive tech.

questions.question: When creating external links with `target="_blank"`, why is it a security best practice to add `rel="noopener noreferrer"`?
options: To prevent the newly opened target page from accessing the opening window object via `window.opener` (preventing tabnabbing attacks)
To prevent search engines from indexing the current website
To force the browser to download the linked webpage as a local PDF file
To disable all CSS styling on the linked external webpage
questions.explanation: Without `rel="noopener"`, the destination page gains a reference to `window.opener` and can manipulate the original tab's location (reverse tabnabbing exploit).

questions.question: Which of the following represents a correct, accessible HTML heading hierarchy structure?
questions.explanation: Headings must follow a logical sequential order without skipping levels downward (e.g., from `<h1>` directly to `<h4>`), allowing screen readers to construct a meaningful outline.

questions.question: Which HTML tag structure is used to create a Description List (glossary or key-value list)?
options: <ol type='desc'> containing <item> and <val>
<ul> containing <li> with nested <label> and <text>
<dictionary> containing <key> and <value>
<dl> containing pairs of <dt> (term) and <dd> (description)
questions.explanation: A description list is declared with `<dl>`, enclosing term items (`<dt>`) and their corresponding definitions or descriptions (`<dd>`).

questions.question: Which HTML entity should be used to display the literal character '<' in webpage text without triggering HTML parser tag errors?
options: <
&lessthan;
&
>
questions.explanation: `<` stands for 'less than' (`<`), while `>` is 'greater than' (`>`), and `&` is the ampersand (`&`).

questions.question: What is the proper attribute syntax in HTML5 to store private custom data directly on an HTML element for JavaScript consumption?
options: custom-* (e.g., custom-user-id="42")
meta-* (e.g., meta-user-id="42")
data-* (e.g., data-user-id="42")
var-* (e.g., var-user-id="42")
questions.explanation: HTML5 specifies the `data-*` prefix for embedding custom data attributes on standard elements, accessible via JavaScript's `element.dataset` property.

questions.question: Which boolean HTML5 global attribute completely hides an element from both visual display and screen reader accessibility trees?
options: invisible
display-none
aria-hide
hidden
questions.explanation: The `hidden` attribute specifies that an element is not yet, or is no longer, relevant, hiding it visually and from assistive technologies (similar to `display: none`).

questions.question: What does the `lang="en"` attribute on the root `<html>` element accomplish?
options: It restricts users from typing non-English characters into input forms
It sets the character encoding of the database server to English UTF-8
It automatically translates any foreign words on the webpage into English
It informs browsers, search engines, and screen readers of the primary natural language of the document for correct pronunciation and indexing
questions.explanation: The `lang` attribute declares the base natural language of the text, enabling screen readers to load correct pronunciation engines and assisting search engines.

questions.question: Which element is used to highlight or mark text for reference purposes due to its relevance in another context (e.g., search results)?
options: <spotlight>
<yellow>
<highlight>
<mark>
questions.explanation: The `<mark>` tag represents text marked or highlighted for reference or notation purposes, typically due to its relevance in a search query or user action.

questions.question: Which Open Graph `<meta>` property is used by social platforms (LinkedIn, Facebook, Discord) to display a preview thumbnail when a link is shared?
options: <meta name="preview-img" content="https://example.com/banner.png">
<meta name="thumbnail" content="https://example.com/banner.png">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/banner.png">
<meta property="social:poster" content="https://example.com/banner.png">
questions.explanation: The Open Graph protocol defines `og:image` as the standardized property for social share thumbnail previews.

questions.question: What is the semantic role of the `<time>` element in HTML5?
options: To pause JavaScript execution for a specified number of seconds
To measure the network latency and loading speed of the current webpage
To represent a specific period in time or a timestamp in a machine-readable format using the `datetime` attribute
To display an animated real-time countdown clock in the browser toolbar
questions.explanation: The `<time>` element represents time or date data, providing a machine-readable ISO format via the `datetime` attribute (e.g., `<time datetime="2026-09-11">`).

questions.question: Which of the following is a classic inline element by default in HTML?
options: <span>
<section>
<div>
questions.explanation:
`` is an inline element that only occupies the width necessary for its content and does not break onto a new line, unlike block elements (`
`, `

`, `

`).

questions.question: Which attribute can be added to an HTML element to allow users to directly edit its text content directly in the browser?
options: interactive="text"
contenteditable="true"
allow-input="true"
user-editable="true"
questions.explanation: The global `contenteditable` attribute transforms any HTML element into a rich-text editable region in the browser.

lessons.lessonTitle: Lesson 3: HTML Forms, Input Types, & Client-Side Validation

questions.question: Which `<form>` attribute specifies the MIME type encoding used when submitting forms containing binary files?
options: enctype="binary/octet-stream"
enctype="text/plain"
enctype="application/x-www-form-urlencoded"
enctype="multipart/form-data"
questions.explanation: When uploading files via `<input type="file">`, the form must use `method="POST"` and `enctype="multipart/form-data"` so the browser splits inputs into MIME parts.

questions.question: How do you correctly bind an explicit `<label>` to an `<input>` element for maximum accessibility?
options: Set the `<label>`'s `name` attribute equal to the `<input>`'s `name` attribute
Set the `<label>`'s `for` attribute equal to the `<input>` element's `id` attribute
Set the `<label>`'s `id` attribute equal to the `<input>`'s `placeholder` attribute
Set the `<label>`'s `href` attribute to point to the input's CSS class name
questions.explanation: Binding `label for="xyz"` to `input id="xyz"` ensures screen readers announce the label when the input receives focus, and clicking the label focuses the input.

questions.question: What happens when a form control has the `disabled` attribute compared to the `readonly` attribute upon form submission?
options: Both `disabled` and `readonly` fields are submitted normally with empty values
Fields with `readonly` are omitted from submission, while `disabled` fields are submitted
Fields with `disabled` are omitted from the form submission payload, while fields with `readonly` are included and sent
Neither `disabled` nor `readonly` fields can ever be inspected via JavaScript DOM
questions.explanation: A `disabled` input is ignored during form submission (not submitted in the payload), whereas a `readonly` input prevents user edits but submits its value.

questions.question: Which HTML5 input attribute enforces client-side validation using a regular expression pattern?
options: validate
pattern
regex
match
questions.explanation: The `pattern` attribute accepts a JavaScript regular expression (e.g., `pattern="[0-9]{10}"`) that the input's value must match before submission.

questions.question: Which HTML5 element provides pre-defined autocomplete options for an `<input>` field while still allowing custom user input?
options: <datalist>
<select>
<autocomplete>
<optgroup>
questions.explanation: A `<datalist>` contains a set of `<option>` elements connected to an `<input list="listId">`, offering suggested autocomplete options without restricting custom entries.

questions.question: How do you group multiple radio buttons together so that selecting one automatically deselects the others?
options: Give all radio buttons in the group the exact same `name` attribute
Give all radio buttons the exact same `id` attribute
Wrap each radio button in the same `<fieldset>` without any names
Set their `type` attribute to `type="radio-group"`
questions.explanation: Radio buttons sharing the same `name` attribute belong to a mutual exclusion group where only one radio button can be checked at a time.

questions.question: Which elements are used to semantically group related form controls together with a visible title or caption?
options: <section> and <caption>
<group> and <title>
<fieldset> and <legend>
<formgroup> and <label>
questions.explanation: The `<fieldset>` element groups related controls in a form, and `<legend>` provides an accessible caption for the fieldset container.

questions.question: What is the default `type` attribute of a `<button>` element placed inside a `<form>` if none is specified?
options: type="menu"
type="reset"
type="submit"
type="button"
questions.explanation: By default, standard `<button>` elements inside a form have `type="submit"`. If you want a button to not submit the form, you must explicitly set `type="button"`.

questions.question: Which HTML5 input type provides a slider control for selecting a numerical value within a bounded range?
options: <input type="number-bar">
<input type="scroll">
<input type="range">
<input type="slider">
questions.explanation: `<input type="range">` renders a slider control allowing the user to select an imprecise or bounded numeric value between `min` and `max`.

questions.question: What does the `novalidate` attribute on a `<form>` element do?
options: It converts all POST requests into GET requests automatically
It bypasses the browser's native HTML5 client-side validation constraints upon submission
It disables all server-side validation checks on backend API endpoints
It prevents the user from typing special characters into any text field
questions.explanation: Adding `novalidate` to `<form>` suppresses browser built-in popup constraint validation messages, useful when handling validation entirely through custom JavaScript.

questions.question: Which HTML element is semantically designed to display the calculated result of a user action or form calculation?
options: <output>
<calc>
<computed>
<result>
questions.explanation: The `<output>` element represents the calculation result from script operations or form calculations (e.g., dynamic pricing or range sliders).

questions.question: Which attribute allows an `<input type="file">` element to accept only JPEG and PNG image files?
options: extensions=".jpeg, .png"
filter="*.jpg, *.png"
type-restrict="images"
accept="image/jpeg, image/png"
questions.explanation: The `accept` attribute specifies a comma-separated list of allowed file types or MIME types that the operating system file picker will filter.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `step` attribute on numerical and date inputs?
options: It controls the animation speed of form transition effects
It defines how many times a form can be submitted before timing out
It determines the tab order when a user presses the Tab key
It specifies the legal number intervals or increments that the input value can jump by (e.g., step="0.01" for currency)
questions.explanation: The `step` attribute defines valid numeric increments (e.g., `step="5"` allows 0, 5, 10, etc., and `step="0.01"` allows cents in financial inputs).

questions.question: Why is client-side HTML5 form validation alone never sufficient for web application security?
options: Modern web browsers charge licensing fees for verifying form constraints
HTML5 input validation only works when the client is disconnected from the Internet
Client-side validation causes severe memory leaks in the browser's DOM parser
Client-side validation can easily be bypassed, modified, or disabled by attackers using developer tools or direct API requests (e.g., curl/Postman)
questions.explanation: Client validation improves user experience, but server-side validation is strictly mandatory because anyone can send raw HTTP requests directly to backend endpoints.

questions.question: Which JavaScript method on an HTML form element can be called to trigger native constraint validation checks programmatically?
options: checkValidity()
verifyForm()
isFormCorrect()
testValidation()
questions.explanation: The Constraint Validation API method `element.checkValidity()` returns `true` if an element satisfies all its validation constraints, or `false` otherwise.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between `<progress>` and `<meter>` elements?
options: `<progress>` represents task completion progress toward a goal, while `<meter>` represents a scalar measurement within a known range (e.g., disk usage, battery level)
`<progress>` only supports binary yes/no states, while `<meter>` supports text inputs
`<meter>` is used for music volume, while `<progress>` is used exclusively for video streaming
There is no difference; both are interchangeable synonyms in HTML5
questions.explanation: `<progress>` indicates completion percentage of an ongoing task, while `<meter>` represents a scalar gauge measurement within a known range (like disk space or temperature).

questions.question: What autocomplete attribute value is recommended for password fields to assist password managers when a user registers a new account?
options: autocomplete="current-password"
autocomplete="generate"
autocomplete="new-password"
autocomplete="create-pass"
questions.explanation: `autocomplete="new-password"` prompts password managers to generate and store a secure strong password instead of autofilling existing credentials.

questions.question: How are form values transmitted when a `<form>` uses `method="GET"`?
options: Sent over a separate background WebSocket channel
Stored in local browser cookies and never transmitted over the network
Included as an encrypted JSON binary payload in the HTTP request body
Appended directly to the destination URL as URI-encoded key-value query parameters
questions.explanation: Forms with `method="GET"` encode input names and values as query parameters in the URL (e.g., `/search?q=term`), making them bookmarkable but visible in browser history.

questions.question: What is the purpose of including a hidden input field (`<input type="hidden">`) with a CSRF token in server-rendered forms?
options: To compress images uploaded by the user before network transmission
To protect the application against Cross-Site Request Forgery by ensuring the form submission originated from an authenticated session on the trusted site
To bypass HTTPS encryption overhead on local development servers
To store the user's plain-text credit card number securely in the browser cache
questions.explanation: CSRF tokens stored in hidden inputs validate that the request was generated by the actual authenticated user and not forged by a malicious third-party site.

questions.question: Which attribute can be set on an input to automatically focus it when the webpage finishes loading?
options: auto-select
autofocus
default-focus
active
questions.explanation: The `autofocus` boolean attribute instructs the browser to place keyboard focus on that specific form control upon initial page load.

lessons.lessonTitle: Lesson 4: HTML Tables, Media Tags & Accessibility

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `scope` attribute on a `<th>` (table header) element?
options: It controls whether a table row is rendered on desktop or mobile devices
It explicitly associates header cells with their corresponding columns (`scope="col"`) or rows (`scope="row"`) for screen readers
It defines the CSS border-radius and background color gradient of the cell
It limits the number of characters that a user can type into table cells
questions.explanation: The `scope` attribute (`col`, `row`, `colgroup`, `rowgroup`) provides clear contextual association between header cells and data cells for assistive technologies.

questions.question: Which HTML attribute is used to make a single table cell span across 3 columns horizontally?
options: span-col="3"
col-width="3"
rowspan="3"
colspan="3"
questions.explanation: `colspan="3"` causes a `<td>` or `<th>` cell to extend across 3 horizontal columns, while `rowspan` merges cells vertically across rows.

questions.question: Which table element pair is used to apply shared styles or attributes to entire columns without repeating classes on every individual `<td>`?
options: <tablegrid> and <gridcol>
<columns> and <column>
<colgroup> and <col>
<thead-cols> and <th-col>
questions.explanation: The `<colgroup>` element and its nested `<col>` child elements allow styling and attribute definitions across vertical table columns.

questions.question: Why should every content image (``) have a descriptive `alt` attribute?
options: To provide alternative text for visually impaired users using screen readers and as a fallback if the image fails to load
To force search engine crawlers to download high-resolution copies of the image
To display an animated tooltip popup when the user hovers their mouse over the image
To prevent unauthorized users from downloading the image via right-click
questions.explanation: The `alt` attribute is vital for accessibility (read aloud by screen readers), SEO indexing, and graceful fallbacks when image requests fail or are slow.

questions.question: What should the `alt` attribute contain for a purely decorative image that conveys no informative meaning (e.g., decorative divider lines)?
options: alt="null"
alt="decorative image"
alt="" (an empty alt attribute)
Omit the alt attribute completely from the tag
questions.explanation: An empty `alt=""` tells screen readers to ignore the decorative image completely. Omitting the `alt` tag entirely is an accessibility error that causes screen readers to announce the raw file URL.

questions.question: Which modern attribute on an `` element enables native browser-level deferred loading until the image is near the viewport?
options: defer="true"
loading="lazy"
fetch="deferred"
preload="none"
questions.explanation: `loading="lazy"` instructs the browser to defer loading images that are below the fold until the user scrolls near them, saving initial bandwidth.

questions.question: Which HTML5 element is specifically designed for 'Art Direction' and serving different image sources based on media query conditions?
options: <image-group> with CSS background rules
containing multiple elements and an fallback
<canvas> with WebGL responsive shaders
<svg-responsive> with embedded bitmaps
questions.explanation: The `` element wraps multiple `` tags alongside a fallback ``, allowing developers to serve different crops or formats (e.g., AVIF/WebP) per screen size.

questions.question: What is the primary role of the `<track>` element inside `<video>` or `<audio>` tags?
options: To adjust playback volume and bass equalizer frequencies automatically
To prevent unauthorized video screen recording on client browsers
To track user watch time and send analytics data to marketing platforms
To specify timed text tracks such as subtitles, closed captions, or audio descriptions (using WebVTT format)
questions.explanation: The `<track>` element attaches timed text streams (like `.vtt` subtitles or captions) with attributes like `kind="subtitles"` and `srclang="en"`.

questions.question: Which attribute is required on an `<iframe>` element to ensure screen reader accessibility?
options: title="Descriptive title of frame content"
caption="Summary"
alt="Description"
aria-frame="true"
questions.explanation: WCAG guidelines require every `<iframe>` to have a clear, descriptive `title` attribute so screen reader users understand what content the embedded frame contains before focusing it.

questions.question: What does the `sandbox` attribute on an `<iframe>` element accomplish?
options: It limits the CPU and RAM allocation of the embedded page to exactly 10MB
It renders the embedded webpage in a high-contrast black-and-white theme
It forces the iframe to load only from localhost testing servers
It applies strict security restrictions (disabling scripts, popups, form submissions, and same-origin access) unless explicitly re-enabled with tokens
questions.explanation: The `sandbox` attribute heavily restricts untrusted third-party iframe content by disabling scripts, forms, popups, and same-origin cookies unless explicit exceptions like `allow-scripts` are added.

questions.question: What is the key technical difference between `<svg>` and `<canvas>` in HTML5?
options: `<canvas>` files are stored in XML format, while `<svg>` is rendered strictly with WebGL
`<svg>` cannot be styled with CSS, whereas `<canvas>` styles are written exclusively in CSS
`<svg>` can only be rendered with server-side plugins, while `<canvas>` is supported natively
`<svg>` is vector-based, retains a searchable/styleable DOM node structure, and scales infinitely without pixelation; `<canvas>` is a raster/pixel-based immediate-mode drawing surface
questions.explanation: SVG is an XML-based vector format where every element is part of the DOM tree and scales losslessly. Canvas is a raster surface manipulated via JavaScript pixel drawing APIs.

questions.question: What are the four core accessibility principles defined by the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)?
options: POUR: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust
REST: Representational, Encapsulated, Stateless, Tiered
CRUD: Create, Read, Update, Delete
FAST: Functional, Accessible, Scalable, Trustworthy
questions.explanation: WCAG is structured around the four foundational POUR principles: Perceivable (users can perceive content), Operable (UI components are operable), Understandable (info is clear), and Robust (content works across tools).

questions.question: What is the foundational 'First Rule of ARIA' in web development?
options: If you can use a native HTML5 element or attribute with the semantics and behavior you require, use it instead of repurposing an element with ARIA
Every single `<div>` must have an ARIA landmark attribute attached
Always add `role="button"` to every `<button>` element to ensure full compatibility
ARIA attributes should only be written in uppercase letters
questions.explanation: The First Rule of ARIA states: If a native HTML element (like `<button>`, `<nav>`, `<dialog>`) already has built-in semantic behavior and keyboard support, never replace it with a `<div>` styled with ARIA roles.

questions.question: What does `aria-hidden="true"` do to an HTML element?
options: It disables all mouse click and hover events on the element
It hides the element and all its children from assistive technologies (screen readers) while keeping it visually visible on screen
It applies CSS `display: none` to hide the element completely from screen and accessibility trees
It encrypts the text content inside the element so search engines ignore it
questions.explanation: `aria-hidden="true"` strips the element from the accessibility tree (useful for decorative icons accompanying visible text) without affecting visual layout.

questions.question: What is the accessibility impact of assigning `tabindex="0"` to a custom element (like a `<div>`)?
options: It forces the element to be the very first focused element when the page loads
It turns the element into an automatic submit button for forms
It inserts the element into the natural keyboard tab navigation order and makes it focusable via the Tab key
It permanently removes the element from keyboard navigation entirely
questions.explanation: `tabindex="0"` places an element into the sequential keyboard navigation flow. `tabindex="-1"` makes it focusable only via JavaScript, while positive tabindex values are discouraged as an anti-pattern.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an 'aria-live' region (e.g., `aria-live="polite"`) in dynamic web applications?
options: It instructs screen readers to announce dynamic content updates (like notifications or status messages) without requiring page reloads
It measures the user's typing speed inside form inputs
It streams real-time audio and video directly through the user's microphone
It forces the browser to refresh the webpage every 5 seconds
questions.explanation: An `aria-live` region notifies assistive technologies of live DOM updates. `aria-live="polite"` waits until the user is idle, while `aria-live="assertive"` interrupts current speech.

questions.question: Why is anchor text like 'Click Here' or 'Read More' considered poor for web accessibility?
options: It increases the file size of the HTML document unnecessarily
It prevents search engines from caching the destination URL
It triggers spam filters in modern web browsers
It lacks meaningful context when screen reader users navigate through an extracted list of all links on a page
questions.explanation: Screen reader users frequently navigate pages using link lists out of context; descriptive text (e.g., 'View Python Full Stack Syllabus') clarifies the destination, whereas 'Click here' is meaningless alone.

questions.question: What is the purpose of providing a 'Skip to Content' link at the top of a webpage?
options: To load the page in low-bandwidth mode by omitting all images and videos
To allow keyboard-only and screen reader users to bypass repetitive header navigation menus and jump directly to main content
To close the current browser window quickly using keyboard shortcuts
To automatically skip past all paywalls on news subscription websites
questions.explanation: A skip link allows keyboard and screen reader users to jump over large navigation headers straight to `<main id="main-content">`, saving significant tabbing effort.

questions.question: Which image format is modern, open-source, and provides superior lossless and lossy compression compared to JPEG and PNG for web delivery?
options: ICO
TIFF
AVIF / WebP
BMP
questions.explanation: Modern formats like WebP and AVIF offer 30-50%+ better compression efficiency than legacy JPEG/PNG while supporting alpha transparency and animations.

questions.question: What does the `playsinline` boolean attribute on a mobile `<video>` element do?
options: It restricts playback exclusively to inline CSS keyframe animations
It embeds the video as an inline base64 string inside the HTML document
It allows video to play directly within the webpage layout on mobile devices (e.g., iOS Safari) instead of automatically forcing fullscreen mode
It forces the video to loop indefinitely with subtitles enabled
questions.explanation: `playsinline` tells mobile browsers (notably iOS Safari) to play the video inline inside the document flow rather than automatically launching a fullscreen media player.
